title: The Murderer at the Door
objective: After this level you can weigh Kant’s claim that you may not lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding against a consequentialist reply.
summary: Constant held truth is owed only to those with a right to it; Kant replied in 1797 that truthfulness is unconditional; consequentialists allow a protective lie.

cards.headline: A murderer knocks and asks if your friend is hiding inside. May you lie?
cards.body: In 1797 two thinkers argued over exactly this doorstep. One of them said no.

cards.headline: Constant’s challenge
cards.body: In 1797 Benjamin Constant attacked a German philosopher who held that lying to a murderer, asking whether your friend had taken refuge in your house, would be a crime. A duty to tell the truth, taken unconditionally, would make society impossible, Constant wrote. Truth is owed only to someone with a right to it, and no one has a right to a truth that injures others.

cards.headline: Kant answers
cards.body: Kant replied in an essay the same year. Truthfulness in statements you can’t avoid is a duty to everyone, however great the disadvantage to you or anyone else. A lie always injures someone: if not a particular person, then humanity, because it makes declarations in general less trustworthy. To be truthful, he wrote, is “a sacred unconditional command of reason”.

cards.headline: Kant turns the tables
cards.body: Kant even used consequences against the liar. Suppose you say your friend isn’t home, but he has slipped out unseen and meets the murderer on his way. Then, Kant argued, you could justly be accused as the cause. Whoever lies must answer for what follows. Tell the truth, and the outcome isn’t charged to you.

cards.headline: The consequentialist reply
cards.body: Consequentialists hold that whether an act is right depends only on its consequences. From Constant to Mill and Sidgwick, many philosophers have held that lying to a would-be murderer is permitted: on this view, a lie that protects a life is the better act. Kant’s answer is that even one exception undermines the trust on which every right founded on contract depends.

cards.headline: The Murderer at the Door: the big picture
learned: Constant: truth only to those with a right to it
Kant: truthfulness is an unconditional duty
Kant: the liar answers for what follows
Consequentialists: a protective lie may be right

questions.prompt: What did Kant call being truthful in all declarations?

options.label: A useful rule with sensible exceptions
A private matter between friends
options.rationale: He called it a duty to everyone.

options.label: A sacred unconditional command of reason
A custom that varies by country
options.rationale: He treated it as a command of reason.

questions.explanation: Kant called truthfulness in all declarations a sacred unconditional command of reason.

questions.prompt: A burglar demands to know whether your neighbours are away. How would Kant and a consequentialist differ on answering falsely?

options.label: Both would require the truth, since burglary is a serious crime
Kant would allow the lie, but the consequentialist would forbid it
Both would say it depends only on how you happen to feel
Kant forbids it; the consequentialist may allow a lie that prevents harm

questions.explanation: Kant held truthfulness to be a duty to everyone whatever the cost; consequentialists judge the act by its consequences, so a protective lie can be permitted.

questions.prompt: Glaucon, in Level 3, argued that people are just only when they can’t safely be unjust. How does Kant’s view of truthfulness differ?

options.label: Kant held truthfulness is a duty however great the disadvantage
Kant agreed that honesty is only fear of being caught
options.rationale: Kant’s duty holds whatever the consequences.

options.label: Kant said truth is owed only to those with a right to it
Kant thought lying is fine if no one finds out
options.rationale: Kant said a lie always injures humanity.

questions.explanation: Glaucon’s ring suggests people are honest only out of fear; Kant held truthfulness a duty to everyone, however great the disadvantage.
